utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning. Could you call the case, please, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-05-88-T, the Prosecutor versus Vujadin Popovic et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, ma'am. All the accused are here. From the Defence teams I notice the absence of Mr. Krgovic and Madam Nikolic. I take it that's for the same reason as yesterday. Prosecution I see is in full force. Mr. McCloskey, Mr. Nicholls, Mr. Thayer. The witness is present in the courtroom, so let's start. Madam Fauveau, you were in possession of the floor yesterday when we broke, when we adjourned.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Sir, at the end of the hearing yesterday we were speaking of your meeting with General Mladic on the 28th of July, 1995. Would you say that General Mladic did not greet you on that occasion because in that period he had realised that the agreement was not being respected by the Bosniak side?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that, and I can't claim either way. My status at the time was that of a prisoner of war and that was my understanding of it.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Yesterday, on page 23 and 24 of the transcript, you said that you cannot confirm or contest that the convoy was escorted by the UNPROFOR. I should like to show you your statement, 5D201, and it should not be broadcast, a statement that you gave to the Office of the Prosecutor in January 1998. In the English version it is page 9, first paragraph, and in the B/C/S version page 8, last paragraph. Would you please see in this last paragraph on page 8, in the middle of the paragraph you stated: "[Microphone not activated] ... with 20 buses. They were escorted by UNPROFOR and were escorted through to Kladanj."

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: In view of the fact that this statement was made at the time that was closer to the events, it is to be assumed that it is more correct than my recollection today. So I could agree with this, if that is what I said in 1998, and that was almost 10 years ago and things are forgotten in the meantime.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] During the hearing of the 30th of March, on page 27 you stated that when the evacuation started the people were afraid and that the families were separated and the men were not allowed to accompany wives and children. You said that the first evacuation included everybody, including men of military age. I would like to know, therefore, is it not true that men of military age who were separated from their families was due to a decision of the authorities in Sarajevo and the military authorities who advised that this offer should be rejected and that they should continue to struggle.

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: There are several questions in what you have said. I shall try once again briefly to say how it was. According to the signed document, the right to evacuation was enjoyed by the following: The wounded, the sick, women, children, and persons under 18 years of age and over, I think, 55 years of age, and they were encompassed by the evacuation. As for everything else, men of military age should have surrendered, and they were not supposed to be included in those buses and trucks that were transporting the population. That's as much as I can say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President. I'd just ask my learned colleague for a specific reference to where the witness's testimony stated that men of military age were actually boarding the buses other than the wounded to which he just referred. I honestly can't find it at page 27. I'm wondering if there is another site that you can point me to where he discusses military-age men other than wounded boarding the buses during the first evacuation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Thayer. Madam Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There's a translation error. What I said was not the first evacuation. It's the first offer for an evacuation on the 13th of July. I see now that there's an error. May I repeat the question? I am sorry. It was not my intention to confuse the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Maybe you didn't get the correct translation in B/C/S, but in the English version there's an error. My question was the fact that the women and children were separated from the men, was this not due to the refusal of the offer made on the 13th of July, which included the whole population?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: This proposal or request, as I have explained, was not adopted out of fear, that this operation of evacuating the whole population may not be carried out in the way the offer was made or, rather, the request was made, and that was the main reason why this first proposal was not accepted -- or, rather, request. And as for everything else, I have explained several times how things happened.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: You were speaking of fear, and in fact you mentioned fear several times during your testimony. Would you not say that that fear was due to three years of war and to mutual mistrust that reigned at the time between the Muslims and the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I could agree with you that this fear was due to lack of confidence, to the period of war that preceded this, as well as the subsequent knowledge as to what had happened in Srebrenica, because the people who tried to get through, some of them came back to Zepa with terrible stories, and this intensified the fear among the people. That is true.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: But it is quite true that on the 13th of July when the first offer was made by the Serbs, you still didn't know what had happened in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, at the time we didn't know. That's what I said in my statement. It was only later, in the days that followed. Maybe the following two, three, or four days.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Nevertheless, the fear was present already on the 13th of July.

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, yes, of course. Yes. Yes. That is the fear that you described as being caused by the war that had raged up until then and the lack of trust, but this fear was intensified as of the 15th following the receipt of information about the fate of certain individuals and what had happened in Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: You said yesterday on page 28 of the transcript that you cannot confirm that people who remained in Zepa experienced anything bad. In the light of what you've said, would you agree that the offer of the Serbs to the civilians in Zepa to choose whether to leave or to stay was sincere?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time the evacuation started this issue was no longer an issue. Whether it was sincere or not, it is a fact that at that point in time there was no possibility of anyone staying to live on in Zepa. That was the real situation, and this was the consequence of all the prior events, the resistance, et cetera. So the moment the evacuation started on the 25th of July, this was no longer a realistic option, nor did anyone give it any more thought.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: At the time when the evacuation started, were there still people who wanted to stay in Zepa?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I am not aware of any.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Sir, you spoke of a meeting of delegates in Sarajevo that you attended in 1993. When you attended that meeting in 1993, did you have occasion to speak about the destiny of Zepa with the authorities of Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: During my visit to Sarajevo, apart from an official event, that is the meeting of the Assembly, a delegation from Zepa had a brief visit with the president of the Presidency at the time, Mr. Alija Izetbegovic. That meeting was quite brief, between 20 minutes and half an hour, and as far as I can recollect, Mr. Izetbegovic asked can we defend ourselves, what the economic prospects were of such an enclosed and small community, but we didn't go into any further details or proposals in that connection. That's as much as I can say about that.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Would it not be probable that the fall of Zepa, as well as the fall of Srebrenica, were agreed on a higher political level and inscribed in an agreement on an exchange of territories?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: We in Bosnia call this the conspiracy theory, but I'd rather not speculate about that.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Sir, could you look at Exhibit 5D201, page 5 in the English version, and page 5 in the B/C/S version as well. In B/C/S it is the third paragraph, and in the English version the fourth paragraph. At the time, in 1998, at least according to what is included in this statement, you said the following: "[In English] Most probably the agreement was reached to have a solution made in which Srebrenica and Zepa would remain in the Republika Srpska. It was probably the only reason why international military assistance was not given to Srebrenica and Zepa." [Interpretation] Sir, is that what you stated in 1998?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. That is what I stated.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I have no further questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Madam Fauveau. Mr. Zivanovic, yesterday I think you don't have any cross-examination --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I not cross-examine this witness, Your Honour. We changed our position. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Same thing, Mr. President. No questions for this witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you so much, Mr. Bourgon. Mr. Lazarevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We don't have any questions for the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Haynes or Mr. Sarapa.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: Just a few questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Go ahead, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, sir. When you're speaking of men of military age in Zepa, are you referring to the troops of the 285th Zepa Brigade under the command of Palic?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, all those soldiers and those who belonged to -- were of that age group and were not members of the 285th Zepa Brigade. There were older men who were not in the brigade, but according to the document signed they were included in the group of able-bodied men of military age. That is the person I referred to.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: You met General Mladic on the 19th of July when certain conditions were conveyed to you, or requests as you call them, which related to the evacuation of the population who wanted to leave and to the disarmament of the 285th Zepa Brigade. Brigade, yes. In view of the fact that no response arrived from your side according to your recollection and what you said in your testimony, you said that this was understood by the Serb side as a rejection and the continuation of the situation which continued until the 24th of July. On that date you met General Mladic once again, and from that day onwards there were no further -- there was no further fighting around Zepa. The combat operations ceased; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Everything you said is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: I have a very short question. Would you agree with the statement that the evacuation of Zepa was carried out between the 24th and the 27th of July?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the 25th to the 27th.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: But has it not been stated that -- didn't you say that the evacuation started on the 24th?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It was on the 24th that the agreement was signed, but the actual process of evacuation started on the 25th.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: In the physical sense, therefore, on the 25th.

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Sarapa. Mr. Thayer, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good morning, Your Honours; good morning, everyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Good morning, Witness.

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I want to begin picking up with a theme touched on by my learned friend Madam Fauveau and also previously in your prior cross-examination. That's concerning the sincerity of the VRS in this agreement that was signed on the 24th and the proposal, as you put it, that was placed before you by General Tolimir on the 13th, specifically the sincerity of the VRS to allow the people of Zepa to stay. Sir, do you know what happened to the mosque in Zepa after the VRS entered the town?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was destroyed.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Josse yesterday suggested to you that the VRS had lived up to its part of the agreement. And that was at page 27, line 15. If we could have 65 ter number 209 placed on e-court, please. And I'm just going to take you through a few documents. Now, sir, the Trial Chamber has already heard testimony concerning the efforts of the able-bodied men of Zepa to try to reach free territory in the weeks after the fall of Zepa. This document is a VRS daily combat report, and if we scroll down we can see who it's from. Lieutenant Colonel Kusic, who was also a signatory to the agreement which you signed, and it's dated -- sorry, go back to the top, please -- August 8th, to the Drina Corps command. Do you see that document?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Let me just read to you in English the first paragraph. "On 7 August in the afternoon, in the canyon of the Kamenica River, five remaining balijas," his term "who were after the fall of Zepa travelling along the following route," and he describes a route, "went down to the railway tracks at Dub and tried to reach Drenovica walking on the tracks were liquidated. The group was separate and had travelled for 10 days." His report continues: "The same day in the vicinity of Luka an unarmed Ustasha born in Srebrenica, 24 years old, was liquidated. Before he died, he said that he fell behind the others and he was looking for food." Sir, killing a lone, unarmed, hungry 24-year-old, does that sound to you like the VRS was living up to the terms of the agreement?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: One, it's a leading question. Two, my learned friend knows full well that this witness cannot deal with this particular document. He has repeatedly said that after he was taken prisoner in late July, he did not know what had happened. This is a deliberate pejorative piece of re-examination and should be stopped now.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I'll rephrase, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. I think Mr. Josse is perfectly right and please refrain to ask questions to the witness referring to a period about which he has already stated that he knows nothing.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Well, sir, this conduct reported by one of the signatories to your agreement, is this consistent or inconsistent with the agreement that you signed?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Is that a question for me?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course it doesn't correspond, because here we're dealing with killings; right?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: If we may have 65 ter number 186 displayed, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Sir, do you see the document in front of you?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do. I can see the first part, the first paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And can you see that it's dated July 29, 1995? It's addressed to the Drina Corps --

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... command post, the Drina Corps intelligence and security organ, and personally to Lieutenant Colonel Kusic, headed "very urgent." I just ask if we can have the bottom of the page displayed so we can see who sent it. Do you recognise the name at the bottom there, sir?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I want to turn your attention - if we could go back up to the top - to the third paragraph. And that's page 2 of the English, the second full paragraph where General Tolimir says: "Continue combat operations in order to surround and destroy the 1st Zepa Brigade until the Muslims make the exchange and carry out the agreement from the 24th July related to their disarmament and surrender. Take all necessary measures to prevent them from leaving the encirclement. Do not register persons you capture before cessation of fire and do not report them to international organisations." Again I ask you, sir --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Next sentence, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: "We are going to keep them for exchange in case the Muslims do not carry out the agreement or they manage to break through from the encirclement." Now, I ask you, sir, do not register persons you capture and do not report them to international organisations, is that consistent or inconsistent with your agreement that you signed on the 24th of July?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is inconsistent with the agreement, because they were all supposed to be registered straight away by the International Red Cross. That was the agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, I have one more document to show you on this topic, sir, and I may need the assistance of Madam Usher to hand out some hard copies. This document does not have a 65 ter number. It was disclosed January 30, 2006.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Your Honour, Mr. Thayer was good enough, and I'm grateful to him for this, to put on our table this morning a list of proposed documents for his re-examination. It includes, I think, eight documents that are not on the 65 ter list.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: If I may respond because I think there is some confusion. The list that I have tendered to my learn friend this morning is not a list that I intend to use in the examination or my redirect examination. Are you talking about packet or the --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: No. I'm talking about this document of -- which includes eight -- eight documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It has been circulated to us too.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Now, Your Honour, it seem --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We -- Mr. Josse, I think we did make -- give a ruling sometime back on whether we expect all documents used on redirect --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Absolutely and -- and what -- if I may briefly finish. I'm not actually going to invite the Chamber to stop the re-examination. All I'd like to do is put down a marker that having heard it in due course, I might then make a submission about the re-examination that has taken place and as to whether these documents should be admitted into evidence. But I accept that sensibly, the Chamber won't be able to rule on that until it's heard the complete re-examination. So I'm not going to interrupt for this purpose again, but I reserve my position.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you so much, Mr. Josse. Mr. Thayer you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I see Mr. Bourgon standing, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. Bourgon. I didn't notice you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President. Regarding what the Trial Chamber just mentioned a few moments ago. Yes, the Trial Chamber has ruled on allowing the Prosecution to use documents which are not on the Rule 65 ter list in re-examination. However, the Defence recalls, Mr. President, that we did file a motion for certification of this decision. We are of the view, and I speak for this accused but also with the other accused in this case. We are of the view that the use of documents which are not on the Rule 65 ter list in re-examination creates a serious prejudice to the accused and go against the right to a fair trial, and in this case, Mr. President, we just for the record this must be mentioned if this is going to be allowed with this witness. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... The record of course. Yes, Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Mr. President, the Defence for Ljubisa Beara also joins Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. In the meantime until we decide the matter of certification or until the matter is finally determined in any case, procedurally our decision still holds good and will continue to regulate the current proceedings until reversed, if at all. Yes, Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. And I apologise to Mr. Josse for interrupting his objection. I thought we were talking about something that he and I were working on to hopefully save some time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, sir we only have this document in English. It is a memorandum from a UN civil affairs office, sector Sarajevo headquarters to UNPROFOR headquarters in Sarajevo, and it is dated 29 July 1995, and the subject is negotiations in Zepa. Page 2 contains the following passage and I'll just read it to you from the English: "Also during the afternoon, I received a message from Ed Joseph in Zepa who indicated that the Serbs were apparently planning to seize a number of Bosnian fighters ('war criminals'), regardless of what agreement was reached. He noted that the Serbs seemed to be using UNPROFOR to entice the Bosnians to give up their weapons and were perhaps using UNPROFOR to give the Bosnians a false sense of security." Sir, does that passage sound to you like it's consistent or inconsistent with the agreement that you signed?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I repeat, according to the agreement they were supposed to be handed over within the circle of UNPROFOR and registered by the International Red Cross. These people being brought in was inconsistent with the agreement that was signed.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, yesterday, sir, Mr. Josse also showed you Defence Exhibit 6D102. It was some kind of transcript of a conversation involving a Mr. Amor Masovic. Do you remember those questions, sir?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do. Only perhaps we need an explanation. I couldn't go into the details until I'd seen it again, so I can't comment.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Well, do you remember -- and I'll just read the section that was quoted to you at page 18, line 9 of yesterday's transcript, that -- do you remember that the document contained the passage: "The all-for-all agreement reached at the airport on 20 July includes the release of all members of the army from all the aggressor's prisons and camps, including the new captives of Srebrenica"? Do you remember that passage being quoted to you yesterday, sir?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, you later testified, yesterday, about how sometime around the 26th of July it became clear that nothing would come of the all-for-all exchange idea, and that was at page 30, line 4. Do you recall that testimony, sir?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I do recall it.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. I want to explore with you the relationship, if any, between these two topics. Sir, do you know what -- or to what degree the fate of the men from Srebrenica became an obstacle to the all-for-all prisoner exchange idea?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I personally did not have all that information in view of the fact that it was all done in Sarajevo. So it's difficult for me to address that matter and comment on all the details, to accept them or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Well, let me show you a couple of documents and see if they correspond at all to your understanding from the information that was filtering to you, on the ground. And I'm going to show you a couple of documents with the assistance of Madam Usher. And this document, as well, was disclosed January 30, 2006, but does not have a 65 ter number. Now, sir, this is a UN memorandum dated 20 July 1995, subject "meeting on prisoners exchange and evacuation of Zepa." Again, we only have the English. In the third full paragraph, there's a reference to the meeting being convened at the Sarajevo airport and Amor Masovic representing the Bosnian government. In the next paragraph, there's a passage and I'll just read it: "No final made because the Bosnians were not satisfied that the Serbs had accounted for all the prisoners taken in the assault on the Srebrenica enclave. The Serbs agreed that they would try to produce a fuller reckoning of the Srebrenica prisoners in the next several hours." Sir, I'll just ask you, did any of the information, reflected in the passage I just read to you, filter down to you on the ground in those days, specifically on the 20th or the 21st?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as about this information, well, not in that form. It didn't reach me. However, we did receive information in other ways. But at the time we relied on the stories told by the survivors, people who had survived, about the events in Srebrenica. But as to official information, I myself did not have them about people being taken prisoner, executed and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Sir, to save some time I had two other documents, but I'll move on based on that -- the answer you just gave. I don't think it will be productive. The next topic I want to touch on with you concerns some questions asked by Madam Fauveau yesterday about the month or two prior to the VRS attacks on the Srebrenica and Zepa enclaves. She put it to you that Zepa was not shelled until July of 1995, and you had some discussion about a -- a calm situation that existed in June and the beginning of July 1995, and that was at page 48, line 12, and page 49, line 14. And, sir, you had some -- some recollection of a village called Pripecak, I think, perhaps, being shelled, but you weren't sure when that was. And that was at page 49, line 15. I just want to show you one document and see whether --

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I'd just like to show you one document and see if it helps you shed any light on this issue. This document was disclosed October 18, 2005, and was specifically referenced in the Prosecution's pre-trial brief at paragraph 173, page 57. Now, sir, this is an UNPROFOR sector Sarajevo weekly situation report for 15 July 1995. Again it's only in English so I'll just read out portions. On page 2 of the English, under the heading "Serb assault on Zepa begins, UNPROFOR forces under attack by the Serbs are powerless," there's a reference in the fifth paragraph down, and I quote: "Throughout the week there had been sporadic artillery, mortar and heavy machine-gun fire directed at the Safe Area's population centres, particularly Zepa town and the villages of Ribioci and," here it says, "Pripecki." Can you help us out, sir? Does it refresh or jog your memory at all about any activity in the first week of July?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes. This report -- yes, I remember it. I remember the village, Pripecak. And this report shows that on the 8th of July, is that right, if I'm reading it correctly, that these attacks were carried out, artillery attacks. Well, that's what I can confirm.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Sir, at the time do you recall receiving any information that the village of Ribioc had been targeted?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's difficult now for me to remember all that. Well, you can see it from the centre of Zepa.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: But if that's what it says in the UNPROFOR report, then that's probably it.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Well, I'm just asking for your recollection, sir, and I'll move on. I want to turn to the next page, the top of the document, and again I'll quote: "UNPROFOR's position in the pocket has also been difficult. The 79 Ukrainians in the pocket have been under Serb bombardment since 27 June, with the tempo increasing this week. "Early in the week, the Serbs tried to force the Ukrainians out of OP 9 at the southern end of the pocket. Later in the week, OPs 1, 2 and 3 at the south-western end of the pocket were also attacked. "The attacks came after ultimatum from the Serbs, delivered on 30 June, that UNPROFOR should withdraw from the pocket immediately." Sir, how does this information that I just read comport with your recollection of the state of affairs militarily in the last week of June or June and early July?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The overall atmosphere at the beginning of July was tense. Now, I can't remember these military activities, but everything was looming in the air. There was a sentiment that something would happen. And this in a way is a demand for withdrawal, UNPROFOR's withdrawal. Well, I didn't know about this earlier on.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. And, sir, just -- just to be clear, and that was the only other question I had on this topic. As one of the civic leaders in Zepa, did you ever receive this information that UNPROFOR had been attacked by the VRS at the end of June and given an ultimatum to leave the pocket? Was that ever communicated to you?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. The last --

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: The last topic I want to address is a -- you were asked a number of questions regarding UNPROFOR failing to interdict smuggled goods and arms and about UNPROFOR, in fact being accused by the VRS of covering up the activities and intentions of the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and that was at page 44, line 1 of yesterday's transcript. And you just heard me read the portion of the document concerning the ultimatum to UNPROFOR from the VRS. Sir, did you become aware in July of 1995 of the VRS exercising further control over UNPROFOR in Zepa, that is military control. And I have hard copies here to distribute of one last document. This has been approved for inclusion on the 65 ter list that was disclosed September 19th, 2005. We just haven't given it a number yet. So my question, sir, is did you become aware in July of 1995 of the VRS exercising further control over UNPROFOR in Zepa?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you be more specific, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: In what way do you mean --

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- because -- may I just be allowed to finish? We otherwise knew that every convoy, including this one, the UNPROFOR convoys, not the UNHCR ones, that the army of Republika Srpska, I assume, had the right to control and did exercise that right. Now, these immediate occurrences prior to the attack on Zepa, I or the civilian section of the organisations in Zepa did not have knowledge of. We didn't have any information that any additional things like that were happening.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. I want to see whether we can be shown the B/C/S version of this document in hard copy. This is a combat report. And if we could just move to the bottom of the document so we could see who it's from, please. From again Lieutenant Colonel Kusic. And if you would just take a look at the paragraph headed "UNPROFOR," and I'll just read out the portion that's in English since we don't have it on e-court. "Check-point number 2 Boksanica, where the UNPROFOR commander is located has been put under the control of our forces. An agreement was reached with him not to attack, with the condition that they should not open fire on our BP," translated as "battle formation," "which he accepted with the request to leave his positions where they are, and he would in return provide information on enemy activity and would not call in NATO Air Force."

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Air force, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Sir, did you receive any information to this effect during the period of time when you were staying at Boksanica during those days?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, Colonel Dudnik only told me that he had been threatened by the Serbs, that he and his soldiers would be killed if a NATO attack were to be made. This is what he said to me sometime around the 26th of July when we were alone in a room at check-point number 2. As for this additional information, that he informed the Serb side about enemy activities, that is the Bosnian side, I was not aware of.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: That concludes my redirect examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I have one question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Judge Kwon would like to put a question to you, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, you were referred to a couple of VRS documents at the beginning of Mr. Thayer's re-examination, one of which is Mr. Kusic's report, and the other being the General Tolimir's order, in relation to liquidating remaining soldiers of Zepa Brigade after the falling of Zepa enclave and not to report the captives -- or not to register them and not to report to international organisation. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I take it that you can answer whether it is consistent or inconsistent with the agreement that has been reached based upon what is written on that -- those documents, but my question is whether you were or you are aware of those situation, yourself.

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I, no. Because the period that these documents refer to was the period when I was already in prison. So I had no information about those events.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Excuse me. That is error in translation. It was translated in the line 5, "I know," but the witness responded not, "I not."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. I was about to clarify that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Zivanovic. Judge Prost? Judge Stole? We don't have any further questions of you, sir, which means you are free to go. The usher will assist you. Before you leave the courtroom, however, I wish to thank you on behalf of the Tribunal for having come over to give testimony in this case, and on behalf of everyone, I wish you a safe journey back home.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Exhibits. Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Your Honour, we obviously have some additions to the tender list which was submitted, and I'll just start with the original list that has been e-mailed to everyone. I'm not sure if 6D00030 still appears on the list. No, it's been taken off. That was something that's already in evidence. Other than that, we would just offer the items that are listed on that exhibit list, in addition to the documents to which the witness was referred today in his redirect examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. The -- I take it that the Defence teams are all in possession of the two lists that have been distributed by the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Thayer, have you used all of these documents listed in the second -- second list?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: No, we have not, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If you could identify those --

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: -- which you didn't use today.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Absolutely. P02500 were not used, and did -- with the Court's indulgence.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I believe that is the second document that was not used.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And you still insist on tendering them?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: No, Mr. President. We'll withdraw those, and we'll need to add, I believe, two others to this list, and I'm just using a process of elimination. Unfortunately, things were moving a little fast last night and I haven't taken a look at this list that's before you. I've only been working with the documents, but I can --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. I think we need to be precise this time since --

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And I can do that, Your Honour, since I have the documents here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I can do that for you. Let's start with the original list which is 2489 and 2490 video footage and transcript. 2491 and 2492 video footage plus transcript. Then 2493 which is a map showing the location of Zepa village, and PIC82, which is a map marked by the witness. Let's start with these. Are there any objections from any of the Defence teams to the admission of these six documents? We hear none. We hear none. So these are admitted. Now we come to the additional list referring to Exhibits used for redirect. The first one is 65 ter number 209, which is the 1st Podrinje Light Infantry Brigade daily combat report signed -- type signed by Rajko Pusic. Is there any objection to the admission of that document? We hear none. Then there's 186. That's a 65 ter number. Yes, Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Mr. President, we do object to the admissibility of all the documents used during the re-examination despite the fact that there is a Trial Chamber's order to the effect that documents can use. I may explain the reasoning now or at the end, whatever the Court prefers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Explain now.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. In order to explain why we object to the admissibility of these documents I simply use one example, and I refer here to page 18 of the transcripts at lines 12 to 14 where my colleague says that in using one of those documents, I don't recall exactly which one it was, but he mentioned that this document was disclosed to the Defence on 18 October 2005, and he also mentioned that this document was referred to in the Prosecution pre-trial brief at page 173 -- or paragraph 173, page 57. Now, our question, Mr. President, is we fail to understand, given the nature of the testimony of this witness, why these -- why this document and the others were not included in the Rule 65 ter list. We also fail to understand why is it that we are given this list this morning without any prior notice. We also fail to understand that there is nothing that was raised in the cross-examination which was conducted by my colleagues, there is no surprise, nothing that the Prosecution could not expect when they decided to include this witness and to call him to testify viva voce before the Trial Chamber. Mr. President, further to the Trial Chamber's order, it appears that we are now on notice that we, the Prosecution, may use any document that was either previously disclosed or even worse, any document that was previously made available to us on the famous or infamous electronic disclosure system, and that is at any time and without prior notice. So we now are facing the situation where there are millions of document out there, and of course we will be asking time to go back and see all these documents, because we need to know the case we have to meet, and at this stage, on the basis of the Trial Chamber's order, we no longer know the case we have to meet. We have to go back, and we have to see every single piece of those documents which the Prosecution can use because they are given the possibility and the permission to use them at any time, how they wanted, when they wanted, with any witness. For all these reason, Mr. President, we object to the admissibility of all these documents used during the re-examination by the Prosecution. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Even those with a 65 ter number?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Not those that have a 65 ter number, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So not all. So we're talking of four. Yes, Mr. Meek.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. Ljubisa Beara also joins that objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Thayer -- oh. Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Perhaps it would be more sensible if I went first, because my submissions are really rather different from my learned friend's.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's deal with this first and then we'll hear your objection, and then we'll decide on everything.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Fair enough, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Just briefly, Mr. President. There's no prior notice about what documents are going to be used on re-direct because there can't be. I'm reacting to doors that were opened widely on cross, and if Mr. Bourgon or any of my other learned friends had objections that it was beyond the scope of the cross, then those objections should have been made at the time and not after the witness has left. I submit respectfully, Mr. President, Your Honours, that every one of these documents was presented in a fair response to questions, issues that were raised on cross. With respect to the 65 ter extremist argument, if I can put it that way, we -- yeah, we draw a complaint when there's a specific reference being made to the pretrial brief or to when the item was disclosed, the pre-trial brief being designed to give the Defence a specific idea of where we're going on a specific issue. This document was referred to in the Zepa section of the pre-trial brief. Once again this is not an issue of millions and millions of documents being -- being thrown at -- at Defence counsel. There is no surprise here. We are -- we are simply responding to issues that are raised on the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. I thank you, Mr. Thayer. Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Very quickly, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: The idea is that's exactly the point that we are making. A document that is used in the pre-trial brief does not find -- make its way onto the Rule 65 ter list of documents. The question is when does the Defence -- when is the Defence supposed to know what is the material that will be used in this case? And we do not know what is the material that the Prosecution intends to use in this case. This keeps us off balance, and this creates prejudice to the Defence and makes this trial wholly unfair. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Bourgon. Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Your Honour, whilst I broadly speaking agree with what my learned friend Mr. Bourgon has said, I accept for the purpose of this argument particularly bearing in mind the previous ruling of this Trial Chamber that the Prosecution are entitled to use documents in re-examination which are not on the 65 ter list, but it's a balancing exercise, and it's not altogether easy for the Trial Chamber to unravel, in my submission, because what the Trial Chamber needs to ask itself is whether the document in question should properly have been used in chief, because the difficulty we face now is how to respond to documents that are dealt with in re-direct. Now, Mr. Thayer is understandably at pains to point out that a given document has been disclosed at any particular time, and that is of some comfort to the Trial Chamber, little comfort to the Defence bearing in mind the number of documents that have in fact been disclosed over the period of time, but what I would invite you to ask yourselves is whether the particular document should have been dealt with in chief, thereby allowing the Defence to deal with it properly in cross-examination, because it's undoubtedly true, and here I agree with Mr. Bourgon 100 per cent, that we need to know the case we are going to meet, and it's not right that the Prosecution responds to the case put to the witnesses in a particular given way. That requires, in my submission, an analysis document by document, frankly, and there perhaps I don't altogether agree with my learned friend Mr. Bourgon is looking at the matter in one global picture as a matter of principle. I would suggest that what the Trial Chamber need to do is look at it more in terms of a document-by-document basis. So that's the way I put it, and I have got submissions in relation to each of the documents that have been used. I don't know whether the Court would like me to deal with those in turn.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think you'd better deal with that, with them now, because I would be asking Mr. Thayer to explain whether he agrees that it was indeed the case of using -- make use of those documents in chief and not in re-direct. I mean, basically this is what it's going to boil -- to boil down to.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Now, so far as 65 ter 00209, and here again I don't agree with Mr. Bourgon, the fact that it's on the 65 ter list doesn't mean to say that the Prosecution can automatically use it with the witness. So I take objection to the use of that particular document because the witness knew nothing about it, and it was inevitable, bearing in mind the evidence that that witness had given, that he would know nothing about it, and to use this witness, particularly for the Prosecution to use this witness as a vehicle to introduce this document is in my submission wrong. So far as P02498 is concerned, could we go into private session for a moment out of an abundance of caution?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Let's do that. Let's go into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are back in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: So far as the sitrep report is concerned, the witness did have some knowledge of that and notwithstanding everything else I've said, I take no point so far as that's concerned speaking personally and in relation to my client's case. Finally, Your Honour, there's the document dated the 20th of July from Mr. Harland, and that again the witness realistically had no knowledge of and was unable to assist and again on that basis I would oppose its admission. So, Your Honour, I hope I've dealt with the matter partly as a matter of principle but also specifically document by document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's abundantly clear, Mr. Josse, and I thank you for being precise, to the point, and succinct at the same time. Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Your Honour, the direct examination I conducted with this witness covered the areas I intended to cover with him on -- on his direct examination. Those were the areas that we intended to elicit. That was the extent of the evidence that we intended to come through with this witness. I was given a stack of approximately a hundred documents that the Defence wished to use and pretty much did use during their cross in which they took him through all kinds of areas that were not covered nor were germane in my opinion to his direct examination. That's why those areas were not brought up. He was shown UNPROFOR documents by Defence counsel, VRS documents by Defence counsel, ABiH documents, newspaper articles. Every manner of medium is presented to this witness and past witnesses, and the practice that we have preferred on this side is to let it in. If -- if a party, and this has been happening from day one with my learned friends, if a party has -- has a document, asks a question, unless there is absolutely no foundation or something unbelievably objectionable about it, we have had no objection. I think we've created that record abundantly here. The -- my learned friends repeatedly will show a witness a document, ask some questions about it, whether or not the witness has ever seen it before, has any familiarity. We've said just let it in. We -- we trust the Trial Chamber. We are ultimately in pursuit of the truth here. We think that these documents meet that burden clearly and that these were not areas that -- that I had intended to go into on direct. I did not go into, but the Defence's cross-examination blew those doors wide open. Just to take one example, yes, Mr. Ed Joseph is on the Prosecution's 65 ter list of witnesses. That doesn't mean necessarily I have to wait six months until Mr. Joseph is here to use a document that perhaps or perhaps not we intend to use with Mr. Joseph. Simply because a document has Mr. Joseph's name on it in addition does not mean it automatically should get a 65 ter number. We exercise a tremendous amount of discretion in terms of which documents get 65 ter numbers and which don't. I don't need to repeat the nightmares we've had in terms of documents not getting numbers, but if the practice were to be every single document that refers to a witness gets a 65 ter number in my opinion would be unfair to the Defence. That would be civil litigation burying your adversary in meaningless documents. What we have tried to present is a streamline list of exhibits and we proceed witness by witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Thayer. I think we'll take the break now. Yes, Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Simply this point about the future witness. It's not just that his name appears on it but he was the source of the information. I'd invite the Chamber to analyse the document carefully in relation to the submission that I made.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PROST
utterances.text: Mr. Josse, I just have one question for you. Do you see a distinction between a document that on its face it might be apparent the witness is unlikely to have any knowledge of it versus a document where the witness may answer that he didn't have any knowledge but it may well have been a different answer?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes, I do see the difference, because I accept what Mr. Thayer has said, that the Defence throughout this trial have cross-examined on that basis. That is how most of the cases in this Tribunal, as far as I can see, are conducted for better or for worse, and therefore the submission that Mr. Thayer makes in relation to that is, I concede, clearly right. The point that I was making was he knew, with respect to Mr. Thayer, that his witness wasn't going to know about those matters bearing in mind the testimony he'd already given in relation to specific comments I made as far as some of those documents were concerned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Josse. Madam Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very briefly, Mr. President. The Defence would like to associate itself to the objections made by my learned friend Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll have the break now, 25 minutes. I don't quite know whether I am going to make it through this sitting, because I'm not feeling well at all, but I'll try. I'll try.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Unfortunately, Judge Agius is indisposed, so we have to sit pursuant to 15 bis. So can I wrap up the situation in relation to the documents which were used during the course of re-examination. I take it that Mr. Bourgon and the associate with other Defence are opposing to the admission of those which had not 65 ter numbers, i.e., the last four documents. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Indeed, Mr. President, and I'd like to add that of course my colleague made some further objections on two documents that are on the list. Now, when the question was asked of me whether I -- my objection stood for those two documents that were on the list, I said as a matter of principle, of course my objection did not stand, but I fully join with the objections raised by my colleague, Mr. Josse. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And to clarify, Mr. Josse, you are opposing to what documents? The first two documents or first document and others? If you'd clarify that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Could Your Honour give me a moment? I'm sorry, I should be clearer, but ... I certainly object to the first two documents, those on the 65 ter list, for the reasons that I have already given. This second document, 2498, I object to also for the reasons I have given. I think I differ from my learned friend Mr. Bourgon in that bearing in mind the previous ruling of the Trial Chamber, notwithstanding the certification request, I can see no basis on which I could object to 2502.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: How about 2499 and 2503?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: 2499, same position as 2502. 2503 is a document that I would respectfully suggest should have been dealt with as part of the Prosecution case or not at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Josse. Having noted the position of the -- each party, the Chamber will mark those documents for identification, and as soon as Presiding Judge will join or the proper witness come and deal with them, we can decide in due course the admissibility. Shall we deal with the Defence exhibits? Who will go first?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'm happy to go first since I cross-examined first, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: A large list has been tendered. I've been helpfully informed that 6D27 which is on our list is in fact already in evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: So therefore it should come off that particular list. To the best of our knowledge, all the other documents are not yet in evidence, and we apply for them to be admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I take it this list is disclosed to the Prosecution as well? Can I hear the position of the OTP on this?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Your Honour, we have no objection to any of the documents on this list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. And we'll then therefore admit them, all of them, subject to those documents which have not been translated yet, and we'll -- no. There are -- those are UN documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: That's right. The only documents that have not been translated are original English language. All the B/C/S documents have been translated into English, so I don't think the problem arises on this occasion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But for those documents as well, those should be translated or not? If you waive --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Well -- JUDGE KWON -- of the Defence --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: We've had problems with the CLSS. I don't want to blame them because they're extremely helpful, they've been very, very helpful with us in relation to these documents. But from recollection certainly on previous occasions and again in a previous case, they will not translate, as a matter of principle, documents in English into B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you for the information. Why don't we leave it at that and we'll admit them all. And Defence Miletic team tendered eight documents.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Chairman, unfortunately there are only two who have been translated. So for the rest we'll ask that they be tendered whilst we wait for the translation into English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Thayer, do you have any say to this?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: No objection to any documents on the list, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So as is written on the list, we'll admit number 2 and 4 and marking for identification the remaining six items. Thank you. Shall we go into private session briefly?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I apologise, Your Honour, for taking us back to the issue concerning the admissibility of these documents on my re-direct. I wanted to just add a couple of words that occurred to me as I was cogitating during the break. I don't think I adequately addressed one other ground that I was trying to make but I don't think I did it, frankly, artfully enough or cogently enough.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And I appreciate that the Court hasn't made its decision yet and I appreciate the opportunity to further address the issue. Particularly with respect to documents about which a witness may not have personal knowledge in terms of the contents, I think what we've seen consistently during the course of the trial, particularly on cross-examination, is that my learned friends have used these documents in such a way to a great extent, and I would say 99.9 per cent of the time without objection. Even if a witness looks at a document and says, "I wasn't there. I don't know about this," or, "I never heard about this," respectfully our position is that that document may nevertheless have utility, have probative value, assist the Trial Chamber ultimately in its decision-making on a particular issue, in that the document itself may complete a picture, may present another side to an issue as it were, even if the witness, him or herself, doesn't have particular knowledge about what was going on in a particular document. Just to use the first document, 209, as an example, here we have events that were going on recorded by a signatory to the agreement. Of course this particular witness had no direct knowledge at the time of this particular individual, but nevertheless we would submit that it is probative evidence of the intentions of one of the signatories to that agreement if you see the actions which are recorded in here. Were we to object as it has been done numerous times on the Defence, I think, number one, that would deprive the Trial Chamber of evidence it -- it ought to consider, and that, number two, it would also really prolong the proceedings if we were forced to think ahead of time of every possible document we may conceivably have to use with our witnesses in our case or our direct examination. We don't want to do that. We don't think that that ultimately is helpful. It will encumber the process, not streamline the process. As I said, we had a very limited idea in terms of what we wanted the Court to understand through this witness's testimony. I showed him one document, I think, and understandably, the Defence had its hundred documents it wished to put through this witness, and again I think ultimately it assists the Trial Chamber in its -- in its search for the truth and its decision-making to have such evidence even if this particular witness doesn't have personal knowledge about the events that are contained therein. I just wanted to clarify that. I don't know if that clarifies it, but I at least wanted to give that a shot. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. The Trial Chamber will note your submission in the future. But as for the Chamber, what was important is that there was no opposition at the time from the Prosecution. Yes, Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. With your leave I'd like to reply to what my colleague just said in addition to the arguments which took place before the break, very shortly, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very briefly.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you. I would simply like to say that there is a difference which my learned friend from the Prosecution omits to mention. There is a difference between examination-in-chief conducted by the Prosecution and cross-examination. When a document is shown to a witness in examination-in-chief, if the witness doesn't recognise the document or the event in the document, I would, of course, object that the witness can testify or say anything about the event in the document because that is examination-in-chief. On the contrary, when we have cross-examination, if the Defence shows a document to a witness, even if the witness has not seen the document, does not know the document, it is a proposition put to him on which he can comment because that might have an impact on his credibility. Now, my colleague says, and I quote on this, he says, "We would not like to be forced to think ahead." Well, Mr. President, that's the complete argument of the Defence. The Prosecution should be able to think ahead and know the case that they are leading before this Chamber so that we know the case we have to meet. The Rules ask of the Prosecution that they produce a list of documents so that we know what material we have to deal with. It is -- that's the duty of the Prosecution to do that. So the fact that they like it or that they don't like it is irrelevant, Mr. President. Now, my colleague said they have a huge discretion in selecting documents. I agree. They have a discretion in many respect. The Prosecution is fully independent. They decide what charges they will lay. They decide what documents they will use. They should live it, Mr. President, in order to make these proceedings fair. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Bourgon. So we'll leave the matter there and come to the point later on in due course. So can we go into private session briefly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good morning to you, Witness. Would you kindly take the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. If you could take a seat.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, in order to protect your identity, you will be called by a pseudonym, which is PW-165, and your image will not be broadcast. Do you understand that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. First thing, if I could hand the witness the sheet which is P02495.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Sir, I would like you to read that piece of paper silently to yourself, don't read it out loud, and then tell us if your name appears underneath the pseudonym PW-165.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-165
utterances.text: Yes, that's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Could that be shown to my colleagues. May we go into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: You are of Serb --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Yes. We are now in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: You are of Serb ethnicity, is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-165
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And did you give signed statements to the Office of the Prosecutor on the 26th of November, 1995, and more recently on the 22nd of March of this year?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-165
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Were you truthful in your statements to the OTP?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Mr. President, I object to the question as to whether a witness was truthful when he gave his statement. This is examination-in-chief. This is a leading question. My colleague said -- he started off with leading questions for identity. Of course we don't say anything for those questions. Now we see that the witness hasn't begun to testify, that he's already saying that his witness is not going to say the truth. Now, there is a matter that will arise with this witness, and my colleague --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I don't follow at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Well, Mr. President, the witness is being -- he's being asked by the Prosecution whether he was truthful in his statement. This is not a 92 ter witness. He's not going to try to get the statement into evidence. He will simply -- he is trying to put the witness on notice because there was an event that took place this week of which the Trial Chamber will probably be made aware later on in his testimony, and I think that the question itself is improper. If he wants -- the witness is there. He is to testify about issues. Let the Prosecution ask about the issues and what the witness knows about the issues and what he saw and nothing else. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Before dealing with that, can I check whether -- with the Prosecution whether this witness is a live witness a 92 ter witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: He's a live witness, Your Honour, and if I can -- I'll answer that question, first.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, please. Mr. Meek.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour. There is an error in the transcript. Page 43, line 22. The witness stated it was 1995 he gave his statement to the OTP. November 26th. I don't believe that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: It should be 2005.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I think any further conversation the witness should take off his earphones off because I know what my colleague is about to say. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Witness, if you could kindly take off your headphones with the assistance of our usher, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And, Your Honour, the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second, Mr. Meek.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Your Honours, if --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Mr. Witness, do you understand English?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Meek was that your concern.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Yes, it was, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Well, first I find it very interesting that Mr. Bourgon didn't ask him to take the headphones off before he made his submission on this exact this issue. Apparently, he wanted the witness to hear what he had to say, but not what I might want to say, although I have no objection to the witness taking his headphones off. Second it's a live witness. I fully expect him to tell the truth. There is to question about that. I think there is nothing improper whatsoever about talking about when the witness made statements and asking if he was truthful in those statements. I know that he's going to be cross-examined on those statements and it's sort of a basic background question. Mr. Bourgon has already alluded to the fact that he's going to cross-examine the witness on these statements and I see nothing improper whatsoever about that question and it's -- I don't recall ever having that question objected to before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Nicholls, the Chamber by majority will allow the question, with my dissent. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: You can answer the question, sir. Oh, excuse me. You need your ... Sorry about that delay, sir. You can answer the question. Were you honest in your statements to the OTP? Did you tell the truth?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-165
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you tell us when you were -- if you were mobilised, when that was in the 1990s?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-165
utterances.text: On the 6th of April, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And which brigade did you join?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-165
utterances.text: The Zvornik Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm going to jump up to 1995 now, July. In July 1995, which unit of the Zvornik Brigade were you in? What was your position?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-165
utterances.text: In June 1995, I was in the military police company.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. And in July 1995?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-165
utterances.text: In July, too, I was in the military police company.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. And how long had you been in the military police of the Zvornik Brigade by July 1995, how many years?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-165
utterances.text: A year and a couple of months.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Who was the commander of the Zvornik Brigade military police in July 1995?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-165
utterances.text: It was Lieutenant Miomir Jasikovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Could we go into private session for one moment, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Let's go into private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: In July of 1995, try to remember who were the security officers for the Zvornik Brigade?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-165
utterances.text: They were Trbic, Milorad, and Drago Nikolic. I'm not sure about the first name of the first person.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Just to be clear then, you're not sure whether Milorad is the first name for Trbic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-165
utterances.text: I'm not quite sure about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, in June and July 1995, could you briefly describe what your primary duties were as a Zvornik Brigade MP? What were your assignments for the most part?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-165
utterances.text: At the beginning of the month of July, I asked for -- to be deployed closer to the town of Zvornik because my wife was in the ninth month of pregnancy, so that I could take her to the doctor's and before a medical commission. So I asked the commander be positioned closer, which he allowed. So that I was appointed at the frontier crossing between Karakaj and Sepak, at the bridge there. And on that day, on the 11th, he called me on the line of the frontier police in Sepak and told me to --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Let me stop you there because I was just asking now about your duties in general. Do you recall the date when Srebrenica fell? Or was liberated, depending on how you prefer to describe it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-165
utterances.text: I'm not quite sure about the exact date.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I want to ask you now some questions about soon after the date that Srebrenica fell. After Srebrenica fell, whatever the date, soon after, did you perform any other duties as a military policeman other than the border crossing duties that you've described?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-165
utterances.text: No. No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: So you're -- to the best of your recollection now, after the fall of Srebrenica, you never did anything except work at a border crossing. Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Meek.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Obviously it's been asked and answered. I object.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I don't think so. I don't agree with you, Mr. Meek. Let the witness answer the question, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you repeat it, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: After the fall of Srebrenica, to the best of your recollection now as you sit there, is your testimony that you never did anything except work at a border crossing? Is that right, after the fall of Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-165
utterances.text: I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: In this time in July of 1995, did you -- what duties did you perform other than working at the border crossing or at Karakaj?

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Your Honour, I again object. Asked and answered. Now he's just asking it in a different -- he's just rewording the same question. He already answered it twice. He answered no the first time, no the second time. I did not, and now the Prosecution is just rewording it and again these objections the witness ought to have his headphones off and I apologise for not asking that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: He is not referring to the different time span?

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: No, same time span, Judge.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: No Mr. Meek needs to listen carefully. Before I was asking about immediately after the fall of Srebrenica. Now I'm about July 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Judge, I object. It's all been --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let's hear from the witness. Proceed, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All of July 1995, what duties did you perform other than working at the check-point by Sepak, at the border crossing?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-165
utterances.text: I also worked in Karakaj and Zvornik in the centre of town at the Sepak crossing.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: In July 1995, did you perform duties as an MP in any towns other than Zvornik and Karakaj?

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Judge, I object. That's a leading and suggestive question, and it's also becoming repetitive. It's again been asked and answered I still claim for the third time and for the fourth time now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: He said he performed working at check-point by Sepak and border crossing, and this question is any -- any town other than Zvornik and Karakaj. Is it not a legitimate question? Mr. Nicholls is referring to other places. Please go on, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
