utterances.text: You can answer the question. Did you work in any other villages other than Zvornik and Karakaj in July 1995, as an MP?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-165
utterances.text: I only worked for that one day when the commander called me when I went to Rocevici and I was active there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. Let's talk about that day. Where were you when you were called to go to Rocevici?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-165
utterances.text: I was at the Sepak border crossing and about 11.00 I was called up by telephone to come to Rocevici, and I went there in a private vehicle, and I found there two or three of my colleagues. I was given an assignment as to what I should do there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: First of all, just to be very clear, you say the commander called you. Give me the name of that commander, just for the record.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-165
utterances.text: The commander was Miomir Jasikovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I'm not asking for the names but your two or three colleagues. Who are you referring to there, when you get to Rocevici?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-165
utterances.text: They were my colleagues, military policemen, but I can't remember their names now.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: What was the assignment given to you by Miomir Jasikovac? What did he tell you to do when you got to Rocevic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-165
utterances.text: My colleagues passed on to me that we should secure a kind of informative check-point and not allow civilians to approach, to check vehicles, and that sort of thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, your colleagues informed you that or it was Miomir Jasikovac who told you to set up a -- this check-point? You said you were given an assignment by your commander.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Who would go first?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: It's the first time I hear about a check-point and instructions to give a check-point. It's entirely a leading question. He said his colleagues were told, and he's talking about an assignment. The assignment might mean or be a certain number of things and my colleague suggests to him when did Jasikovac tell you to set up the check-point?

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... And again maybe we need to ask the witness every time to take his headphones off when we make these kind of objections. Maybe you could help me with that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I would prefer the evidence to flow, but I take the point, and if Mr. Nicholls to rephrase the question, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: You stated that on this day your commander gave you an assignment. What was the assignment that he gave you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-165
utterances.text: He told me by telephone that I go to the school at Rocevic and together with my colleagues, at the entrance to the yard, that we should check who was coming and going and to secure that place.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Right. And my question was, again just to be very clear, that assignment to secure the place, the yard, who gave you that assignment, your colleagues at the school or your commander?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-165
utterances.text: I was given the assignment by telephone by the commander, but before that I was told by my colleagues because they were there before I arrived.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, again, best you can, explain the purpose of what you were going to do there. You said to check who was coming and going and secure the place. Which place are you securing, and who are you checking coming and going?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-165
utterances.text: Place was the main village road leading off from the main road about 400 metres towards the school. There was a house there, and the two of us were there controlling the cars, the people who were coming, and telling the civilians to keep away from the yard.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, describe when you first get to Rocevic and the school? What do you see at the school? Who's there? What's going on besides your two or three colleagues from the Zvornik Brigade military police?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-165
utterances.text: When I arrived there there were many civilians, about 20 to 30 of them. They were shouting. They were there to the -- standing to the side, and we were making sure that they wouldn't approach. We didn't enter the school. Other soldiers were in there, soldiers I didn't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: What -- when you say civilians, which civilians are these? Are these Serb, Muslim, Croat? Who are these civilians you're talking about?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-165
utterances.text: They were civilians of Serb ethnicity.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Were they saying anything? How were they behaving? What were these civilians doing?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-165
utterances.text: They were very angry, nervous. They were swearing. They were shouting. They lost many of their own relatives during the war, their brothers and cousins up there, and then they were very bitter and against this group.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Which group were they bitter against? Who were they angry at?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-165
utterances.text: The group of these prisoners who were there in the school.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And what ethnicity -- or where were these prisoners from? Who were these prisoners?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-165
utterances.text: I don't know exactly where they were from, but most probably from the area of Srebrenica, and they were of Muslim ethnicity.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Why do you say most probably from the area of Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-165
utterances.text: Most probably from up there, from Srebrenica, because in that period of time there was nothing else happening anywhere else.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And again, to the best of your recollection what period of time is this? When is this in July that these Muslim prisoners are being held in the school in Rocevic? If you don't remember the date, that's okay, just best you can.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-165
utterances.text: When I got there this was after 11.00, about 11.30 when I arrived. That was about the time. And I stayed there until 1700 hours, something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. What I'm asking now is about the date in July. Do you know what the date was in July? If you don't know, that's okay. Just tell me best you can when it was that these Muslim prisoners were being held in Rocevic school. And if you think it would help you to look at your statement, let me know.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-165
utterances.text: The date is the 11th when I was called by my commander to come there. That was that one day when I was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And how -- what makes you think this was the 11th of July that Srebrenica prisoners were being held at the Rocevic school?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-165
utterances.text: I don't understand the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Why are you saying it's the 11th of July? How do you -- what is making you remember that this is the 11th of July that these prisoners were being held at the Rocevic school, these Muslim prisoners?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-165
utterances.text: I remember the day that I was there. I can't remember any other dates.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: But I'm asking you how you remember that date. Is there any particular reason? Your grandmother's birthday? I mean anything.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-165
utterances.text: No, no. There's no other reason.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And let me ask you if you remember talking about when this happened in your statement. Do you remember talking about that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-165
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Do you remember when in your statement you said it was that you were sent to the Rocevic school to guard Muslim prisoners from Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, I object because you overruled the objection earlier that when he asked this witness if he told the truth in his statements, and apparently now he's wanting to do something different. If he told the truth in his statement, then he's here to tell the truth under oath, and he's already three, four times a page now we've asked about the date. He knew it was the 11th.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Speaking for myself, it is absolutely legitimate to rely on the statement to refresh the memory, so please --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please proceed. Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: If the witness wishes to look at his statement and feels it's necessary, Your Honour, not simply because the Prosecution wants to show him the statement. There's a difference. And I note that at line -- my colleague asked him before, "If you need to look at your statement, please let me know." I haven't heard the witness inform the Prosecution that he's interested in seeing his statement yet. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think that was the case, but I have to consult with my colleagues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The Chamber finds the question absolutely legitimate, and I'd like to reiterate on behalf of the Chamber it is important to have the evidence to flow unless there's a serious concern or objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness -- thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I'm going to read you from paragraph 5 of your statement, Witness, from 2005. "I cannot recall exactly what --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Bourgon, what is it?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I don't agree with the procedure that's being used by my colleague. If the witness wishes to see the statement, then he can give the statement to the witness. Witness can look at it and then answer the question. But he cannot quote from the statement and say, "Do you agree that this is true or not?"

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Show him the statement --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: -- to refresh his recollection but not more than that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a moment. Hold on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The Chamber is of the view that if the witness wishes to take a look at his own statement, it's fine, but there's no problem for the Prosecution to read out the proper part from the statement. But why don't you put the statement to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Can I proceed the way we have this entire trial and just read out the paragraph and then --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Does the witness have the statement in front of him?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: No. I can give him a copy of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let the witness have the statement in his own language, and if you could indicate the part, relevant part. And so that if you indicate the para number or page number so that the witness can follow.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Witness, this is paragraph 5 of your very short statement. I'd like you to read that to yourself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You can read out the part.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: "I cannot recall exactly what the date was that I received this this assignment. This was the one and only time that I performed any sort of guard duty regarding the school in Rocevic. It must have been soon after the fall of Srebrenica, because the school was being used on this day to house prisoners from Srebrenica." Tell me when you've read paragraph 5.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-165
utterances.text: I've read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, has that helped you recall when this event occurred? Think about it. Please tell me. It's the last time I'm asking to ask you. When were you at that school in Rocevic performing this duty?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-165
utterances.text: It was it the 11th of the month of July.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: To the best of your recollection, what was the date of the fall of Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-165
utterances.text: I can't recall that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: You started talking about this check-point or place you set up on the road between the school and the main road. What is that main road? Can you just describe the main road? Where does it go from and to?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Hold on, Witness, a second.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: What is the objection?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Is my colleague quoting from --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: -- that if my colleague thinks it's necessary, he ask the witness to turn off -- take off his headphones because there's been on/off practice on that side.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Witness, if you could kindly take off your headphones. Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: If my colleague thinks it's necessary.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Can I hear you, Mr. Bourgon, now.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I just wanted to say is now my colleague quoting from the statement which I object should not be used the way it is being used right now, or is he saying -- referring to the testimony of the witness? The question from my colleague was: "You started talking about this check-point." I did not hear the witness say "check-point" before, and then I did not hear the witness describe between the main school and the main road. Now, that's in the statement. Is my colleague quoting from the statement, or is my colleague referring to a previous answer? That's my only thing, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PROST
utterances.text: Mr. Bourgon, there was a statement by the witness referencing the check-point, and there was also a statement by the witness referencing the main road in the previous testimony. I can find you the transcript lines.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: At least the witness referred to checking cars and coming and going. Is that not a check-point?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I'm trying to use normal words, Your Honour. I was quoting from his answer, and I can't find it right now rolling up, but my recollection is the same as Your Honour's, that he talked about setting up this place where he's going to check cars and people, and that it's between the main road and the school. Page 53 line 2, "A place was the main village road leading off from the main road about 400 metres towards the school. Two of us were controlling the cars, the people who were coming." That sounds like a check-point on the way to the main road.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: I think the objection, though, went to -- if you go back and look at what the Prosecutor just quoted, Judge, it is obviously not the question he asked, and that question he asked is leading and suggestive because the witness has never, never mentioned the road was between a school and the main road or where it went to or where it went from. I mean, just didn't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I don't see much point of the objection, and it was dealt with, and the Prosecution has a sufficient base -- basis to put that question. So the objection denied. Please proceed, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. Could we please put up in e-court --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I apologise. Please let the witness have the headphones on. Yes, proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Sorry about all this, Witness. I know it must be frustrating to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Could we please have P02494 on e-court. That is a map.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: That should appear on the screen in front of you in a few minutes, Witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, Your Honours, this map does not have a 65 ter number, but I e-mailed it to all of my friends last week, I think. It's very similar to a map - thank you, that's the correct orientation - which does have an a 65 ter number, number 1748, and I received no objection to using this, and I spoke with Mr. Bourgon, and he does not object.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I don't see any rising on the part of the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Witness, can you take a look at this map and try to orient yourself to it? Let me know if you can't see it clearly. And do you recall that I showed you this map when we met earlier?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-165
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. Can you tell us in the centre of this map which -- which area? Can you tell what's depicted on this map?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-165
utterances.text: It's the village of Rocevic, by the main Zvornik-Bijeljina road.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. And is that the same main road you were talking about earlier, when you said that this place where you were checking cars was set up in between the main road and the school?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-165
utterances.text: Yes. It's about 3 to 400 metres upwards towards the school from the main road.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Sorry, I lost interpretation for one second but it's back. Okay. On this map, and we can blow it up if you need to, can you -- well, what would you call this place where you were checking cars and checking people coming through? What term would you give to that post? What was your assignment? What was it called when you were assigned to go somewhere and check everybody coming in and out? How should we refer to that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Nicholls, you can fairly refer to check-point. Can I draw the attention of the Defence to page -- line 19 to 21 of page 51. The witness said, "my colleagues passed on to me, that we should secure a kind of informative check-point and not allow civilians to approach us," et cetera. Please go on, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Can you mark on this map where the check-point was set up by you? And the usher will show you how to use a special pen. Just draw a line across the road where the check-point was. And we can make it bigger if you need it bigger.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-165
utterances.text: Here. On that road.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. And if you can see the approximate location of the Rocevic school on this map, could you circle it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-165
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. And for the record, the witness made a short horizontal line against -- on the road showing where the check-point was in between the school and the main Zvornik-Bijeljina road. Now, were you alone? I think you -- I don't want to -- sorry. Witness, could you please write your number, 165, in the top right-hand corner of this map.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-165
utterances.text: Which number? Would you repeat it, please?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-165
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Maybe the witness could just confirm that the mark he made about the road, that's not the main road. It's a road beside that. This will avoid questions on cross-examination. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: That's fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Could you indicate -- well, could you -- on the main road could you draw an arrow in the direction of Zvornik and label it with a "Z", and an arrow in the direction of Bijeljina and label that with a "B", if you can.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-165
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. I think that's clear. Thank you. That shows Zvornik to the left, as we're looking at it, and Bijeljina to the right; correct? That's what you've drawn?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-165
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I'm finished with that. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Save it and proceed, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: You talked about your colleagues. Who was with you when you were manning the check-point until, you said, approximately -- I think you said 1900. Or 1700. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-165
utterances.text: I can't remember the name of my colleague, but there was just one person at the check-point. The others were separating the civilians from the yard and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And just quickly, why were they separating the civilians from the yard? What were they preventing the civilians from doing?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-165
utterances.text: The civilians wanted to enter the school, probably for some sort of revenge, because during the war they had lost their nearest and dearest, their brothers and cousins, and so they were very angry. And these colleagues of mine, one or two of them, separated them up there, and we were -- the rest of us were up at the check-point.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, as far as you know, were your colleagues successful in protecting the prisoners in the school from the civilians, or was anybody -- or were any prisoners hurt or killed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-165
utterances.text: Well, certainly they were successful in preventing them not to reach the school, and other people whom I didn't know, other members, were providing security at the entrance.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, during the time up to 1700 at the check-point, who passed through that check-point while you were on duty?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-165
utterances.text: At one point while we were at the check-point, myself and another colleague of mine, several -- a couple of vehicles passed by, and one of the vehicles stopped down there for a moment and my colleague said to me, "The security guards have arrived," like Trbic and Drago Nikolic. I didn't see them myself, but I heard that later on one of my colleagues turned up and said what they had been told, that everything must be kept under control. And then they left in an unknown direction.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: The colleague was told by whom that everything must be kept under control?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-165
utterances.text: The security guards there, Trbic and Drago Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Which direction were Trbic and Drago Nikolic coming from when they arrived at the check-point?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-165
utterances.text: Well, from where we were at the check-point, we couldn't see the main road, so we couldn't really establish where they were coming from.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And -- so they were coming from somewhere on the main road in the direction towards the school; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-165
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And then which direction did they continue on?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-165
utterances.text: Well, they came from the direction of the main road, the main road.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yeah. They come from the main road. They get to the check-point, and then they go ...

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness kindly be asked to speak up, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Since they'd issued those orders and checked what the situation was like there, they went through the check-point again, by the byroad, to reach the main road.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, when answering could you come close to -- closer to microphone and speak up. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, I want to be very, very clear about this. You've talked about these vehicles coming. What did you see at the check-point when Nikolic and Trbic, Drago Nikolic and Trbic, were there?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: This question has been asked and answered very precisely. He said exactly what happened when the cars went there. He saw what his colleague told him, what he did not see, and what those cars did. So we're just repeating over and over again the same evidence. Now, I refer, Mr. President, to page 64, lines 11 to 7 -- 11 to 17.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: He said that, "I didn't see them myself, but I had heard that later on --" one of my colleagues ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So, Mr. Nicholls ...

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The witness has said that he had -- just a second. He didn't see them himself, so in light of the statement, if you could rephrase your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: My question, Witness, is you said you didn't see them. What exactly did you see? Talk about vehicles, which vehicles? What did you see at the check-point when they came?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-165
utterances.text: I was there controlling, with my colleagues, the civilian cars which were passing by the village, and there's a wider space there, and a vehicle passed by and parked a little way away by the stadium, next to the school, and the colleague that went there said the security officers or security guards have arrived and have checked what the situation is like and issued orders that no civilians were to be allowed to approach. And after spending several minutes there, they came back and went down towards the main road. So those are the vehicles.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And do you recall -- if you can, describe the vehicle. If you don't remember the vehicle, just say you don't remember it, this vehicle that stopped by the school.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-165
utterances.text: I don't remember that vehicle.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, Witness, do you recall meeting with me last week and talking about this part of your statement? Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-165
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Tell me if you recall, what did you tell me then about seeing Drago Nikolic at the check-point?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Mr. President, the question has been asked. Twice he has described that he did not see Drago Nikolic. I know what my colleague is referring to. Maybe, Mr. President, we ought to have the witness leave the room and we will sort this out once and for all, exactly what when happened last week when I met with the witness and then my colleague asked a number of questions and told the witness many times not to lie on the stand. That's what we have to do. We need to get the witness out of the courtroom so we can argue this matter. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We think before you made that objection you should have asked the headphones of the witness be taken off. So, Mr. Witness, could you take off your headphones again. I had the impression that Mr. Nicholls was trying to refresh his memory, rely on his statement, but what's the point of your objection? Could you tell me again, Mr. Bourgon?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. My colleague asked twice already what the witness did, what the witness saw when he was at that check-point. In the first answer I referred to -- I referred the Trial Chamber to, and that was on page 64, lines 11 to 14, he said, "I did not see Drago Nikolic." Then when my colleague asked the question again, despite the objections of the Defence, the witness repeated exactly again that he did not see him, and that the car parked away from him and that he was told this information by a colleague. Now -- then my question -- my colleague goes on and he asks, "Did you recognise the car?" "I don't recognise the car. I can not tell what car it was." But all this in mind -- with all these answers, now my colleague wants to cross-examine the witness by saying, "What did you tell me in my office last week?" That's my objection, Mr. President. This is inadmissible the way to lead a witness. If my colleague wants to say that this witness is hostile to his case, that this witness is not telling the truth, then of course he can trigger that procedure and then he'll be allowed to cross-examine the witness. But the way my colleague is proceeding is inadmissible. He has had two answers already. Now, I also refer, Mr. President, and that's very important because if you look in the statement that is in front of the witness, it doesn't say that he saw him. It says exactly the same thing as the witness has answered twice already, and now he wants to go back to a conversation that took place in his office last week. Now, that's my objection, was that if we want to go back to this conversation in the office we will, but we will go in detail without the witness being present, and we will go with the information note that was produced by my colleague concerning what happened at that meeting, exactly who did what and when. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Your Honour, first of all, could we go into -- I know the witness has his headphones off, but could we go into private session for this discussion a little bit?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: What's the reason, Mr. President? Is there something about private about the witness that needs to go into private session?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let's hear from the Prosecution first of all.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: If my friend could just relax a minute and let me explain --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a sec. Let's go into private session first of all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Open, yes. Mr. Witness, we are going to take a break, and we will resume again around five to 12.00. So if you could excuse yourself from the courtroom, please. Five to 1.00, correction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So the Chamber will suggest that -- as follows: We'll hear Mr. Nicholls' submission in private session, and we will, if necessary, we'll make public that part later on.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Now, let's go into private session now briefly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The Chamber has decided to hear the submission in public session, and we don't think that Mr. Nicholls has to repeat his earlier submission. We begin with Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I will be as brief as possible. This submission, Mr. President, is being made, of course, on behalf of my client as we are in this trial, like everybody else in the courtroom, in the search for the truth, but it is also being made, Mr. President, on behalf of witnesses whom we believe are being pressured by the practices of the Prosecution before making their testimony before this Tribunal, and this is certainly the case of this specific witness. The relief I ask with this specific witness is simply that we continue with the evidence that is on the record and we move on to another topic, and it's as simple as that. I ask for nothing more. In support of this submission, however, it is important to go into what exactly happened. I will not -- I will spare the Trial Chamber going into the exact contents of the witness's answer, but we do have one answer of the witness at page 64, lines 11 to 17. We have a second answer of the witness at page 66, lines 14 to 21, and we have the statement of the witness which is before the witness, and in all three cases the evidence that is provided by this witness is consistent that he did not see Drago Nikolic. Nowhere does it say that he saw Drago Nikolic at Rocevic school on that day. In this sense, Mr. President, we simply say that it is completely inappropriate to try and go back to a meeting that took place last week, but I need to answer to elaborate as to why it is improper to go back to this meeting. This meeting, Mr. President, was triggered by the Defence. As we normally do for witnesses whom we like to try and get some clarification from, we send a letter to the Prosecution, and we ask the Prosecution please show the letter to the witness, there are issues that we would like to share with them before their testimony to make things easier for all parties in the courtroom, and we simply ask that the letter be shown to the witness, and the witness decides whether he wants to meet with the Defence or not. Most of the time witnesses will -- will decide to meet with the Defence and to discuss the questions that we have. Sometimes it does happen, like it happened one -- in one case earlier in this case, where a witness refuse, and that was raised in the cross-examination which I conducted on behalf of the client. In this specific case, Mr. President, I selected -- I asked the Prosecution that the letter be shown to the witness. It was, and the witness accepted to meet with the Defence. The meeting took place at my request. I said I'd like to meet the witness alone, and I met the witness with my colleague, and we ask -- we put some questions to this witness. On the basis of the statement which is now before the Trial Chamber, which says that, and I can quote, it says that Drago Nikolic -- maybe I should quote just for the sake of completeness. From the statement it is mentioned, and I'll quote from paragraph 10 of the witness statement where it says: I performed my duties at the check point until approximately 18.00 hours. During this time --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you hold on a minute so that we can have the statement in front us.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: By all means, Mr. President. I will be referring to the statement during cross-examination anyway so I don't mind the Trial Chamber being aware of the information that is there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You refer to --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Paragraph 10 of the statement, and that is 3D97. May I proceed, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. At paragraph 10, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: On the basis of paragraph 10 which states during this time the security officers from the Zvornik Brigade Drago Nikolic and Trbic and then first name is either Milorad or Milan came through the check-point and where they were travelling from and the rest. On the basis of this sentence my first question to the witness when I met with him was did you see the car, can you tell me the car looked like. He says, I don't remember the car. I asked him, did you look into the car. Said, no, I didn't look into the car. I said, did you speak to anyone in the car. Said, no, I did not speak to anybody in the car. I said, thank you very much, this is what I will try to get from you on the stand, and that was the end of the meeting, after which I clarified one more issue with him which was where exactly was Sepak border and how he could get a phone call from the brigade because there's no communication between standard, the command of the Zvornik Brigade and this Sepak border. The meeting was very casual and everything went fine, and we were about to leave in less than half an hour. We left the place. The Prosecution then immediately, and I say immediately, in the minutes that followed, met with the witness and this gave rise to the information report that I will now put before you, which is 3D102. If we can zoom in to the last paragraph, and the Trial Chamber may look at the first paragraph and say that this is the context and I agree with the way the context is depicted in this paragraph. And where it says in the paragraph 2 it confirms that we were there for approximately 30 minutes. Probably a bit less.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We should not broadcast this.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: No, not broadcast. And the witness was asked by the Defence -- if the Defence treated him well, and he confirmed it. Now, at this point in time questions were put to the witness in terms of what was discussed with the Defence. Did the witness -- did the Defence bring anything up that I should be aware about, and the witness mentioned, and you can see what is written there, and the witness confirm exactly that the Defence, whether he remembered anything important about Nikolic Drago, and he answered that they asked him about his presence at the check-point, when Nikolic and Trbic passed, pertaining to paragraph 10, and particularly whether he approached the car with the security personnel when it passed and (redacted) denied to the Defence that he approached the car and that was paragraph 10 of his statement. Now, up until that point everything is okay. The Prosecution asked to say, what did you discuss with the Defence? We believe that it is improper for a party to ask what they discussed with another party. For example, I would never, when I meet a witness in these circumstances, I would never even attempt to ask, what did you discuss with the Prosecution? And if you ask this witness here if that would be required and to what happened at the meeting, he would tell you that the first thing I mentioned to him was whatever you said to the Prosecution is none of my business. I have my own question, and I have only very few questions, and then we went into the car and that was it. So the first thing we believe it was inappropriate for the Prosecution to ask what discussed with the Defence. That's the first issue. The second issue, and where it gets complicated, is that when Prosecution was inform of this, two things happened, or, rather, three things happened. First, the witness confirmed that -- sorry. I read from -- I read from lines one, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight -- or seven. It says paragraph 10 of his November statement was read back to him in which he states that Nikolic and Trbic came through the check-point. And then the witness was asked whether this statement was truthful, and the witness said yes, it is. Again, no problem. He is again saying exactly the same thing that is in his statement. What he told the Defence is the same thing. But of course the Prosecution is not satisfied with this answer. They want him to have seen my client. So what happens then, if you look at the last line -- now, this document was drafted, by the way, by the Prosecution. You look at the last line where it says the Prosecution told the witness on several occasions during the conversation that he should remember to tell the truth when on witness stand. Then of course he asked, "Did you see him?" "Yes, I did," and the witness is shaking because he's being contradicted and he is being pressured by the Prosecution telling him you have to tell the truth on the stand many times. There was no problem until then. After this, what happened is we were served with this document in which it explains the situation, in which it says that the witness was nervous when he met us, which is absolutely untrue. And you can ask the witness. The meeting was very casual and very short. There was no nervous. The only -- the only thing about being nervous in this case is the witness being pressured by the Prosecution, knowing that he's about to say something that is favourable to the Defence. The Prosecution is pressuring him by saying that he has to tell the truth and by saying -- by showing him a statement which does not even say that he saw my client, and then he said you better tell the truth. Once we were served with this document the next day, we asked to meet with the Prosecution simply to resolve the matter in a -- hopefully in a friendly manner, and we did have a meeting, and that was my colleague and myself. We met with Mr. McCloskey and his colleague, and we simply discussed. We said, Listen, this is going to be a long trial. We're going meet witnesses. We believe that it is improper that you ask the witness after I see him what I discussed with him. I would never do that. We were informed that this was absolutely normal and that for them this was a normal procedure, that they are able to ask any questions about anything that the witness might have discussed with the Defence. We believe, Mr. President, that this is -- is inappropriate. This is really placing witnesses in a very difficult situation. In my opening brief to this case, I explained to the Trial Chamber, and I gave examples, of witnesses being met by the Prosecution in which they are pushed in terms of saying, "You have to tell the truth. You have to tell the truth." I don't have the references to my opening brief, but there were names of witnesses there and persons that did interview these witnesses and that put pressure on them when the answers they get are not what they would like to have. Now, in a case like this, Mr. President, the witness shows up on the stand after all this debate. We agree to disagree that of course now I know now that whatever I ask to a witness the Prosecution will immediately jump on the same witness and try to say, "What did you discuss with the Defence? What did we miss in our case? Because we miss our documents on the Rule 65 ter list, but that -- we're allowed to do that. So we're going to jump on the witness and ask him the witness what he discussed with the Defence." Now, the witness shows up and begins to testify before a Trial Chamber. There is no difficulty. He answers quite honestly to the Prosecution, and he repeats what he said to me, what is in his statement, and there is no problem. We get to the issue where it is improper for the Prosecution at that point in time to say, "We met in your office and you said differently." Because when the witness met differently -- there are three things he said differently because he was pressured to say differently. He said differently we have a document before you that is unsigned that does not constitute a statement, and the question has already been answered, and the fact that the answer is different would amount to cross-examination, even more than cross-examination. It is really saying, you're not telling the truth. Well, if the Prosecution wants to say you're not telling the truth, then they have to declare the witness hostile to their case. Now, it hasn't happened yet. He hasn't said that he has not said the truth, but he cannot put that question without first going through the motion of saying I'm telling you you're not telling the truth and I ask the Trial Chamber to declare you hostile to my case. In such a situation he can put the questions he wants to the witness. Other than that, the evidence is on the record, and we should move on. Thank you very much, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: A couple of questions, Mr. Bourgon. The first one will be as to whether a party can cross-examine its own witness. You are of course of the view that that should not be allowed.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Indeed, Mr. President. And I have read your dissent in the Milosevic case that in your own personal capacity as a Judge you believe a party should be able to cross-examine a witness. I'm aware of your position; however, as I stand here trying to protect the rights of my client, my position is that, no, a party cannot cross-examine its own witness because this is not what the Rules say for. This is not the practice of this Tribunal, and this is not whatever it is in continental law system or common law system, it is not proper for a party to cross-examine its own witnesses. But as I've mentioned, there are exceptions. One of these exceptions is when the witness is not being truthful to have him declared hostile, which is a completely different -- different approach to -- to a witness, because then the Trial Chamber must take into account that what will happen then, there is a relationship between the witness already is believed to be not credible. Now, I would add that, Mr. President, on this issue that with respect to cross-examination, when I will cross-examine this witness I will also highlight the fact, and this is probably my -- the thing I understand -- I have the most trouble understanding. This witness is contradicted by plenty of Prosecution evidence that was disclosed to us. I will go through every piece of it during my cross-examination. I will show in my cross-examination, and I'm not going to -- we're in public session now so I'm not going to get into this, but I will refer to Prosecution evidence both on the record and Prosecution evidence that is intended to be on the record which show that Drago Nikolic, my client, was not in Rocevic school on that day and now they insist on putting pressure to a witness, a witness by the way who has been here now for 15 days and has -- really, he has had it and he wants to go home, and we're going to put pressure on this witness to get evidence that is contradicted by their own case. Their own case, Mr. President. We have evidence that will show and now we have an expert witness, we've received a report which shows that Drago Nikolic was on duty at that specific moment at the headquarters. And I will say that to the witness, and the witness of course will say, "I don't know." So why is it that we are putting pressure on a witness to get a piece of evidence that is not even a critical piece of evidence that just contradicts the Prosecution's own case? When I talk about the practices of the Prosecution, this is what I'm referring to, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. My second question won't be necessary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PROST
utterances.text: Mr. Bourgon, I'd like you to address the law on the question of having a witness declared hostile. Do you agree with the submission from the Prosecution as to the procedure, as to the test? Can you submit on that? Mr. Nicholls made some submissions and made reference to the Limaj case as to the procedure and to the determination, and in particular, can it be previously oral statements as well as written statements which can form the basis for the declaration?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: In this case, Judge, I will simply answer that I've read that -- that decision in that case, and that was Judge Parker, and Judge Parker is a Judge who, in my humble opinion, is very well aware of the issue of hostile witnesses, and I believe that the test that he articulated then is the right test. Now, this test has to be that the decision for a witness to be declared hostile, the decision, of course, belongs to the Trial Chamber, but there has to be an application for this purpose. The application must be made by the party leading the witness -- or the party, sorry, calling the witness. In this case, the Prosecution is calling this witness before they have to make an application and explain why they want to have the witness declared hostile. In this case, I can tell you very openly that if the Prosecution would even ask to get the witness declared hostile, I would say, On what basis? What is the basis? What basis do you have to have the witness declared hostile when the witness has his statement, is saying something that is consistent with the statement, and has given two answers which are uncontradicted by anything? So I would object to the Prosecution saying, you and me met in my office last week and on this basis I would like to declare you hostile, because he's not telling the truth. Because everything else he's done up to now when he met with the investigators, that was untruthful. When he met with the Defence, that was untruthful. What he said today on the stand, that was untruthful. I don't think there would be any basis for that to allow to get into evidence that took place in the office. And, of course, I would explain and ask the party, the Prosecution in this case, explain to the Trial Chamber what is it -- why is it that they believe that the answer in the office is being untruthful? And I would say that when the Trial Chamber would look at all this material and look at the context in which this pressurised -- the witness is being pressurised into saying, Yes, I did see him. I would say that this should not be put to the witness. It is unfair, not only to the proceedings, but is also not the right procedure for witnesses. We go at -- you know, we really spend lots of attention trying to care for witnesses. What this witness -- the situation he's being placed in, that is improper. It is not right for the Prosecution to do this. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Before I request Mr. Nicholls to respond to this, but I think at this point of time there would be no point for the witness to wait for the hearing, so we can fairly let the witness go to the hotel and rest. Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Bourgon. Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. We, as Mr. Bourgon said, generally, whenever the Defence -- when they've come here and they've asked to meet a witness --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Excuse me a minute. How about bringing in the witness again and giving him a warning not to contact anybody else.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think that's safe.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Given the time spent for the procedural matters, I would expect the parties to try to finish this witness tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Mr. President, before the witness puts his earphones on, can we reassure him this has nothing to do with him personally at this stage. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. We are in open session, yes? Mr. Witness, I apologise to you for having kept you for long outside. We had to deal with some procedural matters, nothing to do with you personally, and things seem to be that we are not in the position to hear your evidence today. So -- so the hearing will be continued a little bit further without your -- without your presence, so I would like you to come again to the courtroom tomorrow morning at 9.00. But in the meantime, could you bear in mind that you are not supposed to contact other people and discuss the -- discuss in relation to your evidence. Do you understand that? Thank you. Have a nice day, and see you tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I understand that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Now -- you may go now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Let's proceed. Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. First of all, I'll try to respond to all of Mr. Bourgon's points other than the last part about what he will do on cross-examination, which I think completely irrelevant at this stage. As he has said, we helped him to meet with this witness and to have a conversation with the witness. The witness told me first that he did not want to meet with the Defence. He told me he had refused to meet with them when they approached him in Zvornik, but we gave the letter to the witness, and the witness agreed to meet with the Defence, and that's fine. And we tried to help to do that. The witness then met with the Defence for about half an hour, and following that I asked the witness, "Everything okay?" As Mr. Bourgon says, he said, "Yes, it is." And the question I asked him, Mr. Bourgon is inaccurate in conveying this as a process where we ask the witness, "Tell me everything that the Defence lawyers asked you. Tell me what your answers are. Give me a verbal transcript of what just happened." I don't think there's anything wrong with that. I think that would be permissible to ask what was discussed. There was nothing cited, no rule, no ethics code which would say that that was impermissible. And honestly, the only thing I could find on point at all was from the Canadian military prosecutor's office, which is where I always turn when I have large ethical issues, and there -- and I'm sure that my colleague does, and they've got a directive which I think is clear, which states that there's no property in a witness. And they -- the directive to the prosecutors' in the Jag is anything you say to the witness, he can discuss your theories of the case, your ideas, scheduling, anything. It's perfectly fine for him to discuss that matter with lawyers for the other party. And the reverse is true. There is no property in the witness and it's fine for me to talk to the witness. And there's obviously no privilege either. It's not a situation where there is any privilege of a Defence attorney talking to a witness. Now, in this case with with my investigator present what I in fact asked the once was you've just met with counsel, Defence counsel, have you remembered anything else that you think it's important to tell me, and that point the witness said to me, yeah, I just remembered that I didn't see him, Drago Nikolic, that day. And at that point, as counsel says, it's in the information report, I read him the paragraph of his statement which talks -- which you have seen, paragraph 10 of Drago Nikolic going through the school. And the reason is the witness this reviewed that document before coming here, said it was all correct, made one correction to the statement in which he talked about not seeing somebody else that is spoken of of the statement, and he said I just want to clarify I didn't see person X in paragraph 12. He left alone paragraph 10 completely. And I'd say the plain meaning when you read that statement he's on duty at the check-point and these people came through. He saw them. So I then asked him, did you or did you not see Drago Nikolic at the check-point? And he said, "I saw him." That's it. That's where we are. And I don't think there was anything impermissible or unethical in those questions. And it's important. There's been a lot of discussion on the other side about ambush. We don't want a trial by ambush. We need to know everything, and that's a two-way street when it comes to witnesses. He doesn't -- they don't need to give me their notes. They don't take statements, they don't give any information before the witness comes before cross-examination but before meeting with the witness I can meet with the witness I believe if that meeting triggered anything that he remembered that he thinks is important. What I really object to, my friend was not at that meeting, and he's talked about all this pressure being put on the witness, and that's just not true. There wasn't any pressure put on the witness. We asked him a question about that, and I did tell him it was important to tell the truth when he testified on the stand. I did tell it to him a couple of times, and that was because essentially what the witness told me was what he had said to counsel wasn't accurate. And I did ask him, "Why did you -- are you nervous? What's going on?" And he said yes I am a bit nervous and he said where he was from. He didn't say he was nervous from what counsel had done. I'm not implying that. He didn't imply that. He just said he's nervous talking about this topic because of where he's from. The question about him being here for a long time, that's true. The witness has been here for a while, but that is something that we asked the witness in advance. We said to him, "Look, we can either reschedule you or you can come but you may be here waiting around a little bit longer than we would like," and the witness made the decision that it would be less disruptive to his life and his career if he just came and got it over with rather than being postponed again. So we do facilitate these meetings. It's okay for us to ask if the witness has remembered anything. We're just trying to get to the truth here. And we do not pressure witnesses in that way. And I think it's -- frankly I don't even understand the argument that telling the witness it's important to tell the truth is somehow putting pressure. Also, I want to note that I have not applied to have this witness declared adverse. I prefer that term hostile, the old traditional term. It doesn't mean the witness is hostile to me, hostile to anybody. What it means is that he is edging away and parting from his statement. What I am trying to do is ask the witness if he remembers what he said to me and to my investigator last week and to give him the chance to remember and think about it, what he saw that day, and answer that question. Now, after that, whatever the answer may be, if I'm permitted to do that, then I may go down the road of requesting to be able to cross-examine him, and I think I would be able under all the relevant law to form a basis for that, but that's slightly down the road. That would be my submission at this time. And finally, Your Honours -- sorry. Mr. Bourgon has said over and over again he told the truth, he told the truth, he told the truth. That's up to you to decide, not up to Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do you have a reply, Mr. Bourgon?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Very quickly, Mr. President. I leave the Trial Chamber the document is there in terms of the paragraph which was written by the Prosecution as to the context of what happened after the witness met with the Defence and what the witness has said today, I leave that up to the Trial Chamber. I would simply reply to the fact that to me it is revealing. I would simply answer to the fact that there is no property in a witness. That's exactly the point that is important. The witness doesn't belong to the Prosecution, and when the Prosecution meets with the witness after the witness has met the Defence it is improper, in my view, to ask the witness what was discussed. You belong to me. You tell me what was discussed, because I'm calling you and you have to tell me what was discussed." This was a way of having to avoid having the Defence even ask for those meeting any more because I know every time I will ask for such a meeting I know that the minute I will be out of the room they will be on top of had him trying to find out what was discussed between me and the witness. My last point, Mr. President --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do you have any basis for that? Not from Canada.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Basis for?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Any jurisprudence as to the impropriety of the --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: To ask because I do not have any legal argument to say that it is improper. To me it is unethical, but unethical because of the pressure that is being placed on the witness. Imagine yourself, Mr. President, being a witness. You come here having made a statement. You meet with the Prosecution. And we have to remember the context of this case and the fact of where the witness comes from. Then the witness agrees to meet with the Defence and he gives an answer which to him is quite normal. Then immediately after he's being asked, "What did you tell them, because you have to tell the truth," and not a couple of time but several time. If that, Mr. President -- if the Trial Chamber feels that this is a proper procedure and this is okay, I stand corrected, but I will say that to me I find it unethical, which brings me last issue, which is the most important issue, and that is to ask this question to the witness tomorrow on the stand would be improper. It would be unfair, and it would simply be harassment to a witness who is trying to do his job by coming here and he's been here 15 days like my colleague said. It would be improper to place him into such a position, because then I will call the investigator who was sitting with the Prosecution, and then the Prosecution will call my colleague who was there in that meeting and we will get to the bottom of exactly what happened. In my colleague said -- wanted to get something else on the witness, then he should have gotten a written statement, and with a written statement maybe he would have a basis to go into the hostile witness procedure. Maybe. Even then I would argue that he was fresh rising on the context that he saying he saw him even if he didn't see him. And that's the most important thing. We're trying to get evidence that the witness saw Drago Nikolic when the witness never said today or before and there are other statements he provided before never said I saw him. He said they came through and he repeated it -- he repeated it to the Prosecution, they came through. He never said that he saw them. That is the crux of the matter thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PROST
utterances.text: Mr. Bourgon, as a point of clarification are you saying that the statement provided by Mr. Nicholls and captured in this information note is false, not correct because Mr. Nicholls has made this representation and it's captured in the note that he did in fact made that statement, the witness made the statement that he saw Drago Nikolic to Mr. Nicholls? Are you disputing that? That the essence of your last comments?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Judge, I think maybe I may not have been as clear as I thought it was. I look at this information report. To me, one, this is not a statement. It is an information report. It is information given to the Defence as to information, and it describes a context. Now, looking at this context and comparing it with the statement, it is your decision, Judge, to decide whether it is proper to place the witness in this context, reading this paragraph, reading his statement and considering his evidence, whether it's proper to call him back in and say, "Listen, I think you lied to the Prosecution" if the Trial Chamber thinks this is the way to go ahead with the witness so be it and I stand corrected. I think it would be improper considering the context of this information report so if it was so important for the Prosecution that they should have obtain a written statement and maybe we would be in a different proceedings today and it wouldn't be how they acted with the witnesses. Putting pressure on the witnesses especially in a case like this. There are lots of witnesses in Zvornik. They are scared unbelievable to come here. They believe that if they come here they will end up in Sarajevo. We have to reassure them that if they come here and say they say the truth and they are not involved in these events that they will not end up in Sarajevo. That's very important. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PROST
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I just feel forced to respond again, Your Honours. We did not put any pressure on the witness. We did not do anything improper --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That's clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: -- if he remembered something and my friend's last comments I think cut both ways. If he believes the witnesses are scared when they come here when they sit down with the Defence attorney who asks him, "okay, I want to ask you what about this paragraph," that can also explain perhaps the answer he gave to them and it's the difference from what he told us. And just the last thing he keeps saying again and again the statement says he didn't see them. I mean, the plain reading of most statements if you say, "I was standing at the door, I saw -- I was standing at the door, Fred came through," you don't necessarily say, "and I saw him walk through the door on his feet." It's -- the plain meaning is he was there. He said he was manning the check-point and Drago Nikolic came through. This was levered possibly into, "oh, I didn't see him, I just heard about it." That's why there's an issue to clear up. That's why I asked the question, "Did you see him or did you not see him?" And he said he saw him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Before we adjourn, Mr. Nicholls, can I ask you that after having heard the witness saying that he had seen Mr. Nikolic there, did you by any chance endeavour to pursue the -- to get the explanation as to his inconsistency in his statement? Did you do that?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, other than just asking --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You just stopped there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: No. I said, "Were you nervous while you were meeting" and he said, "Yes, you know, I'm nervous because of where I live and being here," and that was -- I took that as the explanation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. In light of the time we will adjourn for the day, and we'll give a ruling tomorrow morning, 9.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 4th day of April, 2007, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 1.44 p.m.,
